c.tagline: Equatorial capital where rainforest meets the Atlantic.

taxi.fareNote: Meters are rare; shared 'taxi-brousse' style sedans run fixed low fares along set routes, while private/hotel taxis and app rides require agreeing the price before departure.

emergency.note: Response times can be slow; hotels/large employers often keep private ambulance and security contacts on hand.

hood_landmark.Centre-Ville: Palais du Bord de Mer, Libreville

avoid.reason: Stay off the beaches and unlit back streets after dark, and skip the poorer outlying quartiers without a local guide — muggings occur.
Pickpocketing in Mont-Bouët market and petty theft in shared taxis — keep valuables hidden and use hotel-arranged transport at night.

hood_desc: The seafront government and business core with ministries, banks, the Presidential Palace and the Radisson waterfront strip; best for first-time visitors who want to walk to sights, embassies and the port.
Libreville's leafy, upmarket residential district favored by diplomats and expats, with quiet streets, good restaurants and grocery stores; suited to longer stays and business travelers wanting calm.
The old colonial-era quarter by the water, home to the cathedral and some of the city's newest boutique hotels; good for travelers who want historic character within walking distance of downtown.
A busy commercial hub of malls, supermarkets and office towers a few km east of downtown; convenient and good value for business travelers who don't need to be beachfront.
A mixed residential/commercial district adjoining Léon-Mba Airport; practical for travelers with early flights or short stopovers who want cheaper rates near the runway.

water.note: Tap water is not treated to potable standards; stick to bottled or filtered water.

transit.pay: Cash (CFA francs) paid directly to the bus fare collector or shared-taxi driver; there is no rechargeable transit card. Fares are low and fixed per route segment, so having small bills/coins helps.
transit.hours: Buses and shared taxis run roughly 6am-9pm; after dark, use hotel-arranged cars or app-based rides (Yango/Heetch) rather than street taxis.
transit.note: Public transport is informal and route knowledge relies on local landmarks rather than published maps; most visitors rely on taxis/ride-hailing apps instead.

train: Transgabonais line (Owendo-Franceville) - freight/limited passenger, not a Libreville commuter option
bus: Intercity bus/minibus "taxi-brousse" stations for Estuaire province towns
ferry: Passenger ferries across the Gabon Estuary to Owendo

transit.m: official airport taxi rank (fixed-price sedan) ~25-40 min to Centre-Ville
hotel shuttle (pre-booked, cheaper than taxi rank)

tip.r: Not obligatory; rounding up or leaving 5-10% at upscale restaurants and for hotel staff/drivers is appreciated but not expected at small eateries.

food.desc: Whole tilapia, capitaine or barracuda marinated in garlic, lemon and chilli, then grilled over coals and served with plantain and pili-pili sauce.

food.desc: Gabon's own lager, brewed in Libreville and served in a heavy 630ml bottle so cold it frosts; ordering one is close to a national ritual.

landmarks: Cathédrale Sainte-Marie
This gracefully towered Catholic cathedral overlooking the Gabon Estuary is one of Libreville's most photographed religious landmarks and a symbol of the city's colonial-era architecture.
Hassan II Mosque
A striking gift from Morocco, this grand white mosque with soaring minarets is one of the largest in Central Africa and a dramatic addition to Libreville's skyline.
Léon Mba Memorial
This monument honors Gabon's first president and independence hero, drawing visitors interested in the nation's founding history and political heritage.
National Museum of Arts and Traditions
Home to masks, sculptures, and ceremonial objects from Gabon's many ethnic groups, this museum offers a compact but rich introduction to the country's cultural diversity.
Pointe Denis
A palm-fringed peninsula reachable only by boat across the estuary, famous for its wild Atlantic beaches, surfing waves, and laid-back seaside escape from the capital.
Église Saint-Michel de Nkembo
Renowned for its wooden pillars carved with scenes from the Old and New Testaments, this unique church blends Christian iconography with traditional Gabonese craftsmanship.
Arboretum Raponda Walker
Named after Gabon's pioneering botanist priest, this lush forest reserve just outside the city lets visitors wander shaded trails through equatorial rainforest.
Marché du Mont-Bouët
The largest and most vibrant market in Gabon, a sensory whirlwind of fabrics, produce, and street food that captures the everyday energy of Libreville life.
Presidential Palace of Gabon
The imposing seat of Gabon's government sits along the seafront boulevard, its guarded gates and grand facade making it a notable stop on any city tour.
Akanda National Park
A short trip from the capital, this coastal park protects mangroves and mudflats that host spectacular flocks of migratory shorebirds against a scenic Atlantic backdrop.

train.note: Gabon's only railway, the Transgabonais, runs domestically from Owendo station (Libreville's port, ~15 km south of the city centre) to Franceville via Ndjolé, Booué, Lastoursville and Moanda. Most departures are overnight but there are no sleeper berths, only reclining seats. No international trains exist.

intl.to: Bitam and the northern border for Cameroon
intl.op: shared bush taxis and minibuses — arranged at the gares routières, no online booking

bus.note: No scheduled cross-border coach line runs directly from Libreville with online booking; long-distance travel to Cameroon typically means shared bush taxis or minibuses toward the Kougouleu/Bitam route to the northern border. Domestically, buses and minibuses leave from Libreville's gares routieres.

intl.to: Port-Gentil (Gabon) - fast boat across the Gabon estuary from the Port Mole terminal
intl.op: local operators — tickets at the terminal, no online booking

ferry.note: No reliable scheduled international passenger ferry from Libreville. Domestic fast boats connect Libreville with Port-Gentil across the Gabon estuary; check operators locally at the Port Mole terminal as schedules and safety records vary.
